books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, Democracy in America by Alexis de Tocqueville

primary_sources: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835, 1840)

stimulus.text: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835): “Amongst the novel objects that attracted my attention during my stay in the United States, nothing struck me more forcibly than the general equality of conditions.” In a later volume (1840) he wrote: “Americans of all ages, all conditions, and all dispositions, constantly form associations. They have not only commercial and manufacturing companies, in which all take part, but associations of a thousand other kinds — religious, moral, serious, futile, extensive, or restricted, enormous or diminutive.”
stimulus.source_note: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1 (1835) and vol. 2 (1840), Henry Reeve translation. Verbatim quotations verified against the Project Gutenberg text (eBook 815).

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: According to Tocqueville, when Americans wanted to build a church, found a school, or spread a cause, they

options.text: waited for the king to act
options.misconception: America had no king; Tocqueville's point is that Americans acted together themselves.

options.text: asked a wealthy lord to pay for it alone
options.misconception: In aristocratic societies a lord might act alone; Tocqueville says Americans formed associations instead.

options.text: petitioned the federal government for funds
options.misconception: Tocqueville contrasts associations with government action; Americans formed a society, they did not wait on Washington.

options.text: formed an association and pursued it together

rationales.A: America had no king to wait on. Tocqueville's contrast is with France, where government acted, and England, where a lord acted.
rationales.B: A lord acting alone is the aristocratic way. Tocqueville says Americans, who are individually weak, act together through associations.
rationales.C: Tocqueville's associations are formed in civil life, without reference to political objects. They do not wait for federal funds.
rationales.D: Tocqueville lists what Americans do through associations: found schools, build churches, diffuse books, send missionaries. Where France would send the government and England a lord, America sends an association.
rationales.general:
1. Read his list. Americans form associations to build churches, found schools, and spread causes.
2. Note the contrast. In France the government acts, in England a lord acts, in America an association acts.
3. Answer from the list. Americans joined together and did it themselves.
Background: Voluntary associations carried much of American reform, from temperance to Sunday schools to missionary societies.
Remember: when a writer lists examples, the list is the argument.
